title: Enforcing a foreign arbitral award in Indian courts
p1:
Winning an arbitration case abroad does not automatically put money in your bank account in India.

But here's something many businesses overlook: a foreign arbitral award can often be enforced directly through Indian courts without starting an entirely new lawsuit on the original dispute.
p2:
Under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, India recognizes and enforces qualifying foreign arbitral awards under the New York Convention framework.

The surprising part? Indian courts generally do not re-examine the entire dispute or decide whether the arbitrator got every factual or legal issue right. Their role is limited to examining specific grounds on which enforcement may be refused.
p3:
For example, enforcement may be refused if the arbitration agreement was invalid, a party was not given proper notice, the award goes beyond the matters submitted to arbitration, or enforcement would violate India's public policy.

A practical takeaway: Before approaching an Indian court, examine whether the award qualifies as a foreign award under the Act, identify the relevant jurisdiction, and prepare the award, arbitration agreement and required supporting documents.

A strong arbitration victory deserves equally careful enforcement planning.
conclusion: Should Indian courts take an even stricter approach when examining foreign arbitral awards, or does limiting judicial interference make India a more attractive destination for international business? What's your view?
